newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST - Ahmsa Q3 seen weak, but worst now over.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Ahmsa Q3 seen weak, but worst now over.

text.p: Mexican steel maker Altos Hornos de Mexico SA (Ahmsa) is likely to post weak third quarter results this week, although going forward this looks like the bottom of the down cycle, analysts said.
Abaco brokerage analyst Bond Snodgrass said he expects the Monclova-based company to report a "notable contraction" in year-on-year operating margins and even more on a quarter-on-quarter basis.
"But this is the bottom," said Snodgrass. "Going forward things will improve dramatically," he added.
Lower export prices, the appreciation of the peso against the dollar, and higher costs, especially energy price increases and higher labour costs, all hurt the quarter, analysts said.

Ahmsa reported a nine-month net of 533.49 million pesos last year against 234.03 million in losses in the same period in 1994. The steel giant said its first half net this year was 2.417 billion pesos, up from a 749 million peso profit in the first six months of 1995.

Mauricio Reveco, steel and mining analyst with Salomon Brothers, said he was not as bearish as other analysts. He said demand for steel in Mexico was picking up and that Ahmsa should show a better product mix.
"The healthier demand will show through in this quarter, especially in flat products, cold rolled steel and some in hot rolled, tin plate and galvanized," he said.
Snodgrass was upbeat moving forward because he felt prices had bottomed out and the peso has weakened against the dollar recently, bringing higher export earnings.

"Most importantly, the recovery of the domestic market will bring much higher margins from now," Snodgrass said, adding that national sales margins had a favorable differential over exports because of service premiums, transport costs and import tariffs.

Another analyst, who declined to be named, said he thought the recovery of the domestic market would not show through in the third quarter results and would only just creep into the financial tables in the fourth quarter.

"Domestic sales will show a slight increase, but it will not be enough to counteract the dip in export prices," he added. "We will probably have to wait until the first quarter of next year for a growth of national sales to come through positively on the bottom line."
